  • [92] Xueyang Zhou, Yangming Xu, Guiyao Tie, Yongchao Chen, Guowen Zhang, Duanfeng Chu, Pan Zhou, and Lichao Sun. LIBERO-PRO: Towards robust and fair evaluation of vision-language-action models beyond memorization. arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.03827, 2025a.
  • [93] Zhiyuan Zhou, Pranav Atreya, You Liang Tan, Karl Pertsch, and Sergey Levine. AutoEval: Autonomous evaluation of generalist robot manipulation policies in the real world. arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.24278, 2025b.
  • [94] Di Zhu, Ziheng Yan, and Fang Wan. ActionUNet: Improving robustness of VLA models with efficient multi-scale fine-tuning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.34982, 2026.

Appendix A Evaluation protocol

A.1 Benchmarks and runs

Table 7 lists, for each benchmark, the development and test episodes, the agent’s limits per episode (Section E.1) and the official test protocol, which we did not run. On RoboCasa365 the reply limit is 100 on composite tasks and 40 on atomic ones, and LIBERO-PRO’s step limits leave out its ten settling steps. The official evaluation of RoboTwin 2.0 covers clean as well as randomized scenes, and that of RoboCasa365 uses its pretraining kitchens. RoboDojo [20] has 42 tabletop tasks for two ARX X5 arms in Isaac Sim, in five dimensions: Generalization (12 tasks, half of whose test episodes add clutter), Precision (8), Long-Horizon (8), Memory (6) and Open (8). RoboCasa365 [59] has kitchen tasks for a Franka Panda on a wheeled base, and we run the 50 target tasks of its leaderboard. LIBERO-PRO [92] perturbs the four LIBERO suites [49]: objects are moved (position), changed in appearance (object), the instruction is reworded (language), or a different task is asked in the same scene (task). We run these four perturbations. The fifth, which changes the environment, is not in the release and has to be generated; we have not run it. RoboTwin 2.0 [19] has 50 tasks for two ARX X5 arms in SAPIEN. We run its clean-to-randomized setting (“hard” on its leaderboard): randomized scenes with clutter, textures, lighting and table height, and instructions from the templates kept for testing (unseen). The test seeds are chosen as in the official evaluation, the first seeds from 100000 whose scenes the benchmark’s expert solves.

Every simulated run uses GPT-6-Astra through an OpenAI-compatible gateway (the real robots’ models are given in Appendix K). The two runs of Table 3 and the two of Table 4 use reasoning effort xhigh, with at most 32,000 output tokens per reply on RoboDojo and 8,192 on RoboCasa365. All other runs use effort high with at most 8,192: the LIBERO-PRO and RoboTwin 2.0 results, the harness comparisons of Table 14, and the RoboDojo Open tasks, whose one run both rows of Table 3 share. In that run, store tools in toolbox, which had passed none of its 30 episodes in an earlier run, was not run again and counts as 0. Two runs kept a larger picture window than that of Section E.1: that Open run (90 and 60 pictures and 10 MB instead of 20, 14 and 8 MB) and the RoboCasa365 run without skills (50 and 30 pictures).

Prompts, tools and skills were built on the development episodes of Table 7, not on the test episodes. On RoboDojo these were five rounds on seed 0 and layouts 0–9 (R0–R4); on RoboCasa365, learning seeds 0–9 and validation seeds 10–19 of the pretrain50 split; on LIBERO-PRO, learning states 0–9 and validation states 10–19; and on RoboTwin 2.0, ten learning and ten validation seeds per task below 100000. Between R0 and R1, which added the first skills and a new motion planner, successes on the 34 tasks outside Open rose from 173 to 251 of 340, and R4 solved 330 of 422 episodes of all 42 tasks. The test episodes differ from the development ones in their layouts and seeds (RoboDojo), seeds and kitchens (RoboCasa365), initial states (LIBERO-PRO), and seeds and instruction templates (RoboTwin 2.0). RoboDojo’s layouts 10–19 are public, while its official evaluation uses layouts that are not. HexaShell has been submitted to RoboDojo’s official evaluation.

A.2 Metrics and comparisons

RoboDojo reports a score, the task progress that each task’s score table defines, and a success rate (SR). As RoboDojo computes them, both are averaged first over the tasks of each dimension and then over the five dimensions. The eight Open tasks therefore weigh as much as the twelve Generalization tasks, and the SR differs from the share of successful episodes. Without skills it is 69.92 for 857 of 1,260 episodes (68.0%), and with skills 85.00 for 1,054 of 1,260 (83.7%). We report the mean and standard deviation over the three seeds. The other benchmarks report the share of successful episodes, and RoboCasa365’s overall number is the mean over its 50 tasks. A paired comparison runs the same episodes twice, and we test it with an exact two-sided sign test on the episodes that succeeded in only one of the two runs.

For each benchmark we list the leaderboard entries on the date given in its table and results reported in papers; we ran no other method. HexaShell-TaskTools’s results come from RoboDojo’s official evaluation and from our retests of its frozen tools (Section 3.4). Leaderboard entries follow the official protocol and papers use their own episodes, often on a subset of tasks or perturbations, so neither comparison with our evaluations is exact. Figure 1 draws the top three other entries of each leaderboard in its own ranking: on RoboDojo [2], Q0-Preview, GO-3 Nano Preview and PyRUA-Lean, by average score on 30 October 2026; on RoboCasa365 [1], Awomo-0.5I, minionx and Axiom-0, leaving out Awomo-0.5V, a second model of the Awomo team; and on RoboTwin 2.0 [3], GO-3 Nano Preview, PrismWAM* and PICA-WAM, by the mean of the easy and hard settings, drawn in the hard setting that we ran. The LIBERO-PRO leaderboard lists only VLAs, the best at 53% over five perturbations, so there the figure draws the three highest results in papers, each on its own cells: HarnessPAI, 96.5% on the position and task perturbations of three suites [77]; ASPIRE with GPT-6-Astra, 96.0% on the same perturbations of all four suites (our mean of its eight per-cell results; 98.8% with Claude Opus 5.5) [53]; and PyRUA-Lean with GPT-6-Astra, 94.0% on 40 tasks with five seeds each [69].

RoboDojo’s leaderboard [2] marks each entry of its agent track as an agent alone or as an agent that directs a learned model. Q0-Preview [64], PyRUA-Lean [69], EmbodiedEvo [45], the RoboDojo team’s GPT-6-Astra agent [88] and HexaShell-Preview, our HexaShell-TaskTools (Section 3.4), are agents alone. GO-3 Nano Preview [4] and WorldScape-R2SI [56] direct a world action model, and PhysicalRSI [35] a VLA.

Appendix B Results on each benchmark

B.1 RoboDojo

Five tasks stay below 17 of 30 with skills: store laptop and headphones (1), hang mugs (7), deposit coin (13), and fill pen holder and organize table (16 each). Among the Open tasks, store tools in toolbox passes no episode (Section I.4). Against Q0-Preview, the best leaderboard entry, the agent without skills is ahead on Generalization, Memory and Open and behind on Precision (52.5 against 58.5) and Long-Horizon (54.6 against 58.5). Against HexaShell-TaskTools it has a higher success rate on 36 of the 42 tasks, the same on four and a lower one on two, plug in charger (30% against 32%) and make kong (0 against 2%); with skills it is higher on 40 tasks and the same on cover blocks (100%) and store tools in toolbox (0).

B.2 RoboCasa365

Table 4 gives the success rates on the 50 target tasks: 18 atomic, 16 composite seen and 16 composite unseen. The overall rate is the mean over the tasks, which weights the three groups 18/16/16 as the leaderboard does. The leaderboard entries [1], as of 1 November 2026, are policies trained on the pretraining data and evaluated on 50 episodes per task in the pretraining kitchens; the results from papers each use their own episodes; ours use the 1,500 test episodes of the pretrain50 split, 30 per task.

With nothing written for any task, HexaShell succeeds in 65.6% of the atomic, 50.6% of the composite seen and 61.0% of the composite unseen test episodes, 59.3% overall. The best leaderboard entry, Awomo-0.5I, reaches 64.4% overall. The agent without skills is behind it on the atomic tasks (65.6 against 86.5) and the composite seen ones (50.6 against 58.8), and ahead on the composite unseen ones (61.0 against 45.2). Of its 610 failed episodes, the agent ended 393 itself, 215 ran out of steps and 2 reached the time limit.

With skills, HexaShell succeeds in 91.1% of the atomic, 85.0% of the composite seen and 80.0% of the composite unseen test episodes, 85.6% overall. On the same 1,500 episodes, the skills gain 466 and lose 72 (p<0.001p<0.001). The largest gains are on tasks at the sink and on appliance doors and buttons: ScrubCuttingBoard (2 to 30 of 30), WashLettuce (1 to 26), LoadDishwasher (3 to 27), PreSoakPan (6 to 30), RinseSinkBasin (4 to 26), TurnOnSinkFaucet (7 to 30), CloseToasterOvenDoor (6 to 28) and TurnOnMicrowave (8 to 29). Six tasks pass one or two episodes more without skills. The run without skills kept up to 50 pictures in the conversation instead of 20, so the gap is not the skills’ alone, though on RoboDojo a larger window made no measurable difference (Appendix D). The weakest tasks with skills are HeatKebabSandwich (10), PackIdenticalLunches (13), ArrangeTea (16), SteamInMicrowave (17), SeparateFreezerRack (18) and MakeIceLemonade (19). Of the 216 failed episodes with skills, the agent ended 159 itself and 57 ran out of steps.

With skills, raising the effort from high to xhigh lifts the successes from 1,229 to 1,284 of 1,500 (136 gained, 81 lost, p<0.001p<0.001). Of the 50 tasks, 27 go up and 13 down. The largest gains are OpenCabinet (17 to 27 of 30), GarnishPancake (22 to 27), PackIdenticalLunches (8 to 13) and StoreLeftoversInBowl (20 to 25).

Every task has a skill written on learning seeds, so with skills the composite unseen tasks are not unseen to our agent, though their kitchens and seeds are. The result with skills is listed on the agentic track of the RoboCasa365 leaderboard (submitted on 31 October and added on 1 November 2026) as our own evaluation on pretrain50 seeds 20–49, not under the official protocol.

B.3 LIBERO-PRO and RoboTwin 2.0

On LIBERO-PRO, with skills, HexaShell succeeds in 1,509 of the 1,560 test episodes (96.7%, Table 8). The 71 tasks with skills pass 696 of 710 and the 85 without pass 813 of 850. Without any skills, on other initial states, the agent passes 78.3%. The test episodes use initial states 20–29. The run without skills uses initial states 10–19: for the 102 tasks without a skill at that point it is the validation round, and for the other 54 a control run with the skills switched off. The difference is largest when the perturbation changes the objects or the task, and on the Goal and LIBERO-10 suites. The paired control of Table 14 isolates the skills on 54 tasks: 252 of 540 episodes succeed without them and 531 with them. Most papers report a few of LIBERO-PRO’s cells. On the six cells used by CaP-X [28], HexaShell reaches 98.0% with skills and 83.3% without, against 77.2% for the best other agent we found. On the eight cells of Harness VLA [90] it reaches 97.4% and 79.0%, against 82.4%. There, without skills, it is below Harness VLA with Claude Code. PyRUA-Lean reports 94.0% on 40 tasks, with no breakdown by cell [69].

Of the 51 failed episodes, 50 ran out of steps or ended for lack of them, 38 at the limit and 12 with finish(no_budget); the other ended with stuck. One task, LIBERO-10’s task 3 under the object perturbation, failed all 10 episodes in all three rounds: there the perturbed bowl is too wide for the drawer to close.

On RoboTwin 2.0, in randomized scenes with unseen instructions, HexaShell succeeds in 726 of the 750 test episodes (96.8%, Table 9), and 36 of the 50 tasks pass all 15. The leaderboard entries of Table 9, as of 30 October 2026, are policies trained on clean demonstrations and evaluated on 100 episodes per task in each setting; the results from papers are agents, each with its own episodes. In the randomized setting the top leaderboard entry, GO-3 Nano Preview, reaches 81.5%. The best result in a paper is GPT-5.6-Sol with skills for a VLA, at 90.4% as reported by OmniBrain-0. Without skills, the learning round already passed 411 of 500 episodes (82.2%). Its seeds and instructions differ from the test, so it is not a paired control, and we did not run one on the test seeds. The skills were revised once, for the 15 tasks that failed in the validation round. On the same validation seeds these tasks went from 126 to 142 of 150 (in-sample). On the test they pass 205 of 225, and the other 35 tasks pass 521 of 525. The weakest tasks are stacking three bowls (11 of 15), and hanging a mug, putting bottles in the dustbin and scanning an object (12 each). Of the 24 failures, the agent ended 14 itself, 7 reached the reply limit and 3 ran out of steps.

Figure 8 breaks both benchmarks down, by task group on RoboTwin 2.0 and by perturbation and suite on LIBERO-PRO. The RoboTwin 2.0 groups follow the verb in the task name. Place: the place_* tasks. Pick, move & hand over: pick_*, move_*, handover_*, put_bottles_dustbin, grab_roller and lift_pot. Stack & rank: stack_* and blocks_ranking_*. Press & open: click_*, press_stapler, turn_switch, open_* and put_object_cabinet. Tools & reorienting: the other nine. The line without skills is the learning round, 10 episodes per task on other seeds with seen instructions. GO-3 Nano Preview is the mean of its per-task clean2random results on the leaderboard, 100 episodes per task.

Appendix C Per-task results

Tables 10, 11 and 12 give the successes of every task. LIBERO-PRO has 156 tasks of 10 episodes each; Table 8 and Fig. 8 break it down by suite and perturbation.

Table 10 counts the successes of each RoboDojo task in its 30 test episodes (seeds 0–2, layouts 10–19), in the two runs of Table 3; in the twelve Generalization tasks, half of the episodes add clutter. The Open tasks have no skills, so both columns share one run of them. Table 12 lists the 14 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks that failed at least one of their 15 test episodes, in randomized scenes with unseen instructions; the other 36 tasks passed all 15.

C.1 Six tasks with and without skills

The tables above count successes; the rest of this section shows how a skill changes an episode. Each case follows one RoboDojo test episode that fails in the run without skills of Table 10 and succeeds in the run with them. The two runs share the model, the reasoning effort, the code and the image window, so the skill is the only difference.

Of the 1,020 episodes outside Open, 234 succeed only with skills, in 25 tasks, and 37 only without, in 16 (Section 3.4). We took six of the tasks with the most such gains, two from each of the Generalization, Precision and Long-Horizon dimensions, leaving out plug in charger, which Section 3.4 describes. Together they account for 110 of the gains and 7 of the losses; the Memory tasks gained 2 episodes in all. For each task we sorted the failures without the skill by their cause, chose an episode with a frequent cause that passed with the skill, and read both of its records in full: the code and output of every cell and the camera images after it. Positions and heights are those that the agent measured or that the arms reported. The records hold no poses of objects, so where an object ended is judged from the images. Table 13 summarizes the six cases.

C.2 Make toast: one pitch from rack to slot

In make toast the robot puts two of four bread slices from a rack into the two slots of a toaster and presses the lever down; full credit also requires exactly two slices left in the rack and the robot back at its origin. On test seed 0, layout 11, the agent without the skill asked the right arm to lift each slice at pitch 60∘60^{\circ}, a pose just out of its reach, and the arm went to the closest reachable pose, which, the tool noted, “tilts what it holds by 5∘5^{\circ}” (cells 8 and 14). The second slice shifted in the fingers on its way down to the left slot; the descent stopped 13 mm short, where the hand opened and left the slice leaning (cells 15–16). While being straightened, it slipped out and fell flat beside the toaster (cell 39). A third slice from the rack took its slot (cells 60–63). The eleventh close on the fallen slice lifted it, at step 1,168, and the agent set it back in the rack. The episode ended at step 1,393 of 1,400, with the slice in the left slot tilted and a partial score of 25 (Fig. 9).

The skill, 65 lines without code, settles the carry before the first grasp. Dry runs are to find “ONE arm and pitch” that reach both a rack slice, with its lift of about 11 cm, and the slots, trying pitch 60∘60^{\circ} first, as in all three development successes, then 45∘45^{\circ} and 30∘30^{\circ}. It warns that “an offered pitch or yaw tilts or turns the held slice”, and that slices kept at the same pitch and roll from rack to slot stayed upright, “6/6 seated”. It also records that a lost slice is hard to make up for: “A flat slice was seated once in 44 low closes (6 runs)”, and a third slice from the rack, tried in four development runs, scored 0 in each.

With the skill, on the same layout, dry runs in cell 7 found that at pitch 60∘60^{\circ} the lift could only be approached, 7∘7^{\circ} off, while at 45∘45^{\circ} the grasp, the lift and the slot were all reachable. Both slices then stayed within 1∘1^{\circ} of pitch 45∘45^{\circ} and roll 0∘0^{\circ} from rack to slot and went in without a block (cells 8–19); success came during robot.home() at step 222 of 1,400. Over the 30 test episodes, successes rise from 15 to 21. In 14 of the 15 failures without the skill a slice fell, in 8 of them, as here, while the agent was correcting a slice that rested tilted, high or on the rim. With the skill, a slice slipped in each of the 9 failures as well. Three of the 4 episodes that passed only without the skill have cluttered layouts. There the agent with the skill judged the rack and the toaster too far apart for a steep carry with one arm, a case in which four development runs had all failed, and lost a slice carried at a pitch of 0∘0^{\circ} to 30∘30^{\circ}. Without the skill, the agent handed the slices between the arms, which the skill advises against: hand-overs passed none of 14 slices in the development runs. In the fourth, the second slice tipped the first during the carry.

C.3 Pack objects into box: a box that needed no straightening

In pack objects into box the robot puts a toy car, an electric toothbrush, a hammer and a shoe into an open box, each with its front to the left; full credit requires all four in “the aligned box” and a return to origin. On test seed 0, layout 14, the box stood about 20∘20^{\circ} off the table’s edges, and the agent without the skill wrote “I’ll straighten it before packing”. Its left hand gripped the near wall, lifted the box and turned it (cells 7–9), then again (cells 14–15). After the arm carrying the car shifted the box, the agent dragged it by the rim to the middle of the table (cells 23–24). There, picking up the shoe beside it tipped the box onto its end (cell 35); righting it took 242 steps (cells 38–50). The cells that handled the box took 500 of the 1,300 steps; the budget ran out at a score of 10, one item placed correctly (Fig. 10).

The skill, 63 lines without code, states what “aligned” meant in the development runs: “A tipped or far-turned box counts nothing (the card: aligned); shifted but upright, items counted (4 successes).” For a moved box it records “Gripping, hooking or dragging a moved box: 13 runs, none restored” and prescribes “Upright, roughly left-right, reachable: new centre, go on”. It has the centre taken once, from the rim corners in a head image “with both arms clear of the box”, and each item carried at a grasp height of 0.93–0.95 m over the near wall, then straight down: the shoe crossing the wall at 0.89–0.90 m “pushed the box 20–40 cm (2 runs)”.

With the skill, on the same layout, no hand touched the box. Warned in cell 3 that three of the pixels it had picked lay “on the robot’s own arm or gripper”, the agent moved the left arm aside and took the four rim corners (cells 7–8). The left arm placed all four items, two of them laid down for it by the right arm. Each item crossed the near wall at 0.95–0.96 m and went straight down, the shoe last, and success came during robot.home() at step 614 of 1,300. Over the 30 test episodes, the task passed 8 times without the skill and 26 with it. Without the skill the agent gripped the box in all 22 failures and in 6 of the 8 successes; in 17 failures it did so before grasping any item, and 21 failures ended for lack of steps. The agent rarely mistook a front: in the 10 failures in which it said where the items’ fronts were, it agreed with the skill in all but one. With the skill the box was gripped in 5 cluttered episodes, never before the first item; the 4 failures, also cluttered, each left the shoe outside, facing the wrong way or partly upright.

C.4 Build tower: a lower pair taken from one side of the table

In build tower the robot stacks two pillars, a long board, two more pillars, a short board, a flat plate and a green prism. The task card gives a score of 10 for the lower layer, 30 with the middle board, and 100 for the full tower, each layer centred and both arms back at their start poses. On test seed 2, layout 10, without the skill, the right arm held the long board aside while the left arm set both lower pillars where the board had lain, at x=−13x=-13 and +13+13 cm (cells 9 and 11). Both had started left of the table’s middle. By cell 31 all eight pieces were stacked and both arms were home, at step 635 of 1,050, but the episode did not end. The agent turned the plate back to its starting orientation and then took the top apart to “try a three-level tower”. It stopped at step 1,029 with a score of 10 (Fig. 11).

The card does not say which pillar goes where. The skill does: “Build each pillar level from one pillar of each side: one that started left of the table’s middle, one right.” It cites three development runs in which one arm placed both lower pillars; none got past the lowest score, although two of them had finished the tower. Its list of common failures adds: “Finished tower, no credit: a one-side lower pair. No cheap repair; prevent it.” Its flow puts the tower centre 7–8 cm farther from the robot than the long board’s start, has each arm bring one lower pillar from its own side, and keeps the board’s landing spot 5 cm clear of the spare pillars: in the development runs, a pillar fetched within 5 cm of the board hit it in 5 of 9 fetches, and one fetched from farther away in none of 18.

With the skill, on the same layout, the agent announced before its first motion that it would use “one pillar from each side in both support levels”. It set the tower centre about 8 cm farther from the robot than the long board’s start, and with the board still on the table the left and right arms set their lower pillars at x=−12.4x=-12.4 and +12.6+12.6 cm (cells 5 and 7). The left arm then laid the board across them. Success came 12 steps into the final home(), at step 545 of 1,050, after 31 cells instead of 45. Over the 30 test episodes the task passed 14 times without the skill and 29 times with it. Five of the 16 failures without the skill had taken both lower pillars from one side; all five stacked all eight pieces and scored 10. No success without the skill and no episode with it had such a pair. A one-side pair was not the only reason a finished tower went uncredited: in five more failures the agent stacked all eight pieces with one pillar from each side and no success followed, once with a lower pillar, in the agent’s words, about 3 cm off centre; four of these then lost a top piece while adjusting the tower. Five of the remaining six reported disturbing the lower board while fetching a pillar beside it, which the 5 cm clearance addresses. The one failure with the skill also finished the tower with one pillar from each side, and stopped at a score of 30 for a reason the record does not show.

C.5 Fasten screws: a clockwise turn that pushes down

In fasten screws the robot screws each of three nuts onto the bolt of its colour, fixed upright on the table (the task card calls the bolts screws). A nut counts once rotated onto its bolt to the required depth with the gripper open; success needs all three and both arms at home. Without the skill, on test seed 0, layout 12, the agent first turned the yellow nut 90∘90^{\circ} clockwise, seen from above, to a grasp height of 0.804 m; its top then measured 0.833 m. The next four turns went counter-clockwise, and the agent wrote: “The nut is rotating, but it hasn’t visibly moved farther down the screw.” At step 1,398, after eleven turns, the top still read 0.830 m, and the agent suspected that “the screw may be turning with the nut”. In all it turned this nut 16 times, 1,590∘1{,}590^{\circ} clockwise and 1,760∘1{,}760^{\circ} counter-clockwise, with no clockwise turn ending below 0.804 m. It stopped at step 1,880 of 1,900 with two pairs fastened, a score of 50 (Fig. 12).

The skill says the “screws” are “bolts fixed to the table” and that a nut “resting on the bolt’s tip” does not count. Its step 4 makes the turn one goto with yaw=-120 and contact=True to a grasp height of 0.795 m, “clockwise from above while pushing down”; step 5 repeats it after a regrip. In the development runs, such a pushed turn “seated or read seated 8 of 11 first placements”, while “first turns ending above 0.800 left 5 of 8 nuts on the tip”. “Turning without pushing is slow”, about 1,400∘1{,}400^{\circ} for one nut in one run, “and counter-clockwise turns undo it”. The skill also gives the measured tops of a seated nut, 0.821–0.827 m, and of one on the tip, 0.829–0.836 m; both yellow-nut readings above fall in the second range.

With the skill, on the same layout, the agent made this turn with the skill’s call in cell 6 (Fig. 12c). After step 5 repeated the turn, the nut’s top measured 0.824 m, and the agent wrote: “The yellow nut is centred and reads at the seated height after two tightening turns.” The red and blue nuts followed alike, reading 0.827 and 0.825 m, and the episode succeeded at step 441 of 1,900. Over the 30 test episodes the task rose from 10 successes to 30. All 20 failures without the skill ran out of steps in the same way: each turned nuts both ways (150 of 474 turns counter-clockwise), 240 of the 324 clockwise turns ended above 0.800 m, and the hands spent 551–1,535 steps at a single bolt. Even the ten successes needed 1,260–1,809 steps. With the skill, all 90 first turns were the pushed turn of step 4, all 385 turns were clockwise, and episodes took 419–1,511 steps.

C.6 Fill pen holder: the end that goes up

In fill pen holder, one hand holds a pen holder while the other fills it with four pens. The task card gives 10 points for a pen “correctly inserted tip-up into the upright pen holder”, 25 and 40 for two and three, and success needs all four in, the holder upright and both arms home. On test seed 2, layout 15, the pens are two highlighters and a black and a white pen, each with a clip. Without the skill, the agent picked the black and white pens at yaw 0∘0^{\circ} and −8∘-8^{\circ}, turned them to roll 178178–180∘180^{\circ}, writing tip up, and reported them “in the holder tip-up”. At step 761 all four pens were in and both arms home, with 339 steps left, yet no success came. The agent then turned the purple highlighter over but never went back to the black or white pen, and stopped at step 1,068 of 1,100 with a best score of 25, the value for two pens (Fig. 13).

The skill replaces “tip-up” with a rule, “A pen counts only CLIP END UP”: highlighters and the gold-clip pen go cap up, but “click and gel pens writing tip DOWN”, citing all three winning development runs and “tip up 0/8”. It states which roll raises the clip (“Roll 0 raises the end the yaw heads to”, “roll 180 the other”) and asks for a left wrist image, which costs no steps: “clip end up?”. Its final checks cover the state of step 761: “Four in, arms home, holder down, no success: a pen is wrong end up or not down”.

With the skill, the agent gripped the holder at pitch 5∘5^{\circ}, the skill’s fallback when 0∘0^{\circ} is refused. It picked the black and white pens at nearly the same yaws but kept roll 0∘0^{\circ}, and each left wrist image showed the clip end up; every pen went in at the first attempt. As the skill prescribes, it set the holder down, moved the right hand with by=(0, -0.08, 0.10) and called robot.home() once: success at step 482 of 1,100, in 22 cells against 74. Over the 30 test episodes, successes rise from 2 to 16. In 20 of the 28 failures without the skill, the score stayed below the number of pens the agent reported in the holder, 13 times with all four in. The agent wrote of placing pens tip up in 25 of the 28, while the two successes had only gold-clip pens and highlighters, which count cap up. All 14 failures with the skill ran out of steps with a highlighter that had slipped, caught on the rim or fallen out of the held holder; the skill itself records that, inserted at the yaw it prescribes, “highlighters stayed 8 of 16”.

C.7 Make kong: a target tile that the task card does not identify

In make kong an opponent arm pushes out a discard, and the robot must “declare a kong with the matching tiles”. The robot’s row of standing tiles ends in a pair; the wall, two stacks of two tiles, lies to the left. The score table requires that the three matching tiles are pushed down, the others stay upright and “the target tile is correctly grasped and placed at the required position”, without saying which tile or where. Without the skill, on test seed 0, layout 11, the agent pushed the three matching tiles face up by step 202. Planning to “bring over the discard”, it picked the discard up in cell 12, then moved it between the middle tile and the table in front of the three: “The discard is on the middle tile, but the declaration has not registered.” After six set-downs, the 600-step budget ran out in cell 30, during a third homing. Neither arm reached for the wall (Fig. 14).

The skill names the tile: “The tile to place is the one you draw from the wall, not the discard: leave the discard where it lies (10 runs that moved it all scored 0).” It also names the place: the top tile of the nearer wall stack “stands on end one tile pitch past the outer pair tile, on the row line”. Since only the left arm reaches the wall and only the right arm the target, the skill’s steps 4–9 hand the tile over: the left arm sets it down, grips it again across its width and stands it on end, and the right arm lowers it 5 cm beyond the outer pair tile’s measured centre.

With the skill, on the same layout, the agent planned to tip the three tiles, “leaving the discard and the other tiles untouched, then take the top tile from the nearer wall stack”. In cell 13 the left arm closed on that tile at 6.5 cm, the width the skill gives, then set it down, gripped it again at a yaw of −90∘-90^{\circ} and stood it on end. The right arm lowered it on the row line at x=0.320x=0.320 m, 5 cm beyond the outer pair tile at 0.270 m. Opening the gripper gave success at step 375 of 600. Over the 30 test episodes, the task rises from 0 successes to 30. All 30 episodes without the skill failed the same way: the agent picked up the discard, first at steps 192–503, and never drew a tile from the wall, though two mention it in passing, once as “the spare stack”. With the skill, all 30 drew the wall tile with the left arm and succeeded at steps 347–397.

C.8 What the cases show

Since the two runs of each episode differ only in the skill, the success with it shows that the agent could perceive and handle the objects of that episode. What it lacked without the skill was a fact about the task, which the skill supplied in a few lines. The facts are of the three kinds named in Fig. 6. Three are success conditions that the card leaves open: which tile to place and where it stands (make kong), which end of each pen goes up (fill pen holder) and when a moved box still counts as aligned (pack objects into box). One is a parameter that only contact reveals: a turn that pushes the nut down, with the measured heights that tell a seated nut from one on the tip (fasten screws). Two concern the ordering of steps: each pillar level is built from one pillar of each side (build tower), and the arm and pitch of the whole carry are settled by dry runs before the first slice is grasped (make toast). In five of the episodes, the agent without the skill spent its remaining steps on a repair that the skill rules out: straightening the box, turning the nut back and forth, moving the discard, taking apart the top of a tower whose lower pair could not be credited, and recovering a fallen slice while a third one took its slot. Each of these facts came from development runs in which an attempt succeeded or failed for a reason that the card does not state. The skills leave other failures in place. With the skill, fill pen holder still fails 14 times, each time with a highlighter that would not stay in the held holder; make toast fails 9 times, each time after a slice slipped; and the one failure of build tower stopped at a finished tower for a reason the record does not show. The make-toast skill also cost episodes: in three cluttered layouts, the agent with it carried each slice with one arm at a pitch of 0∘0^{\circ} to 30∘30^{\circ} and lost one, whereas the agent without it handed the slices between the arms, which the skill advises against, and succeeded.

Appendix D Paired comparisons

Table 14 collects the paired comparisons we ran. Each changes one thing and runs the same episodes twice.

The skills have the largest effect we measured (Section 3.4). At effort high on RoboDojo they gain 228 episodes and lose 60, from 615 to 783 successes. The 54 LIBERO-PRO tasks of the control are those that got a skill in the first round, 54 of the 65 tasks that failed at least one learning episode.

Raising the reasoning effort from high to xhigh helps in all three comparisons we ran. On RoboDojo without skills it gains 120 episodes and loses 68, and with skills, on 33 tasks, it gains 116 and loses 54. On RoboCasa365 with skills it gains 136 and loses 81. All three are significant (p<0.001p<0.001). Insert key is left out of the second comparison because its skill differed between the two runs. For the same turn of the same episode it costs 2.4 to 3.3 times the reasoning tokens (Section I.5).

Three changes to the harness, each compared at effort high, made no measurable difference. Keeping up to 90 pictures in the conversation instead of 20 gained 109 episodes and lost 96. Remembered findings (Env_ICL), an object beside robot that records what earlier cells found and what went wrong, gained 99 and lost 91. Measuring an object again after it is put down, where the hand put it, gained 106 and lost 108. In each of these comparisons 15 to 19% of the episodes changed outcome, in both directions alike. Two runs of the same episodes therefore differ in many episodes even when nothing that matters has changed, and a comparison of totals over a few hundred episodes cannot separate a small effect from this noise. Env_ICL is off in every run of Tables 3, 4, 8 and 9.

On the code of round R0 and its 420 development episodes, we compared our system prompt with one taken from the manual of another open agent framework. Ours solved 223 episodes and the other 198, so we kept ours.

Appendix E Implementation details

E.1 Agent loop

The model has two tools: python(code) runs one cell, and finish(status, summary) ends the episode. A reply may hold several cells, which run in order. The status of finish gives the reason: no_budget when the steps left cannot cover another attempt, stuck when there is no way forward, and keep_partial when another attempt would put a partial result at risk. The episode ends when the benchmark ends it, when the model calls finish, or at a limit on replies and time: 100 replies and 90 minutes on RoboDojo, and 40 replies (100 for RoboCasa365’s composite tasks) and two hours on the other benchmarks. The benchmark ends an episode on success, which it checks after every action, or when the step budget is spent. The scene is then judged as it stands. A step is one simulator action (0.04 s of simulated time on RoboDojo).

Pictures are sent as JPEG images. The model’s gateway accepts 8 to 10 MB per request, so only a window of pictures stays in the conversation. The start pictures on the task card are always kept. When the others pass 20 pictures or 8 MB, the oldest are replaced by a short placeholder until 14 remain. Two runs used a larger window (Appendix A). Dropping several pictures at once keeps the cached start of the conversation valid for longer. The loop also supports Claude models and open models served with vLLM.

E.2 Robot API conventions

Positions are in metres in the benchmark’s world frame and angles in degrees. Pixels are (column, row) from the top-left corner. Pitch 0 points the hand level and 90 points it straight down. Yaw turns the hand about the vertical and roll about its own axis. look attaches the current pictures to the cell’s result, optionally with a pixel grid, marked points, outlines, or an enlarged crop. The labels on a crop stay in full-picture pixels, so a pixel read off any picture can be passed to the other calls as it is.

A benchmark adds calls only where its robot can do more. On RoboCasa365 the base drives (drive), and doors and lids turn about their hinges (arc, push_arc). A helper there picks a round dish by its rim (rim_pick). LIBERO-PRO also has arc. Both benchmarks also hand the cell the raw depth picture (depth).

E.3 Perception

The design grew out of the task tools of HexaShell-TaskTools (Section 3.4), which triangulated objects between calibrated RGB cameras inside each task’s own code. Here one service and one set of geometry serve every task, with depth where a benchmark renders it.

One SAM 3 service [14] runs on each machine and serves every episode there. A picture is uploaded once and then named by its hash. Words find by appearance only. Left or second do not pick an instance, so the model chooses among the masks by their centroids or points at the one it means.

RoboDojo has no depth camera, so measure works from outlines alone. A mask in one picture fixes a cone: the rays through its pixels, down to the table. To find the same object in another camera, the service is asked again, with the same words, or with clicks along the middle ray of the first outline at several heights above the table. Each candidate is scored by how well the two cones contain each other’s outline, and colour breaks near ties. The object then lies in the space that every camera able to see a point shows inside its outline, a visual hull that is probed along the pixels’ rays. Its top is the lowest height that still explains almost all outline pixels. Its footprint comes from the surface points each camera sees below the top. A rotated rectangle fitted to the footprint (cv2.minAreaRect) gives the object’s size and grip_yaw, the yaw that closes down-pointing fingers across its narrow side. Pixels that show the robot’s own arm do not count against an outline. They are found by drawing the arm’s meshes at the current joint readings. With one camera the height cannot be measured. The object is then taken to rest on its support, and the result says so and gives a wrist pose that would add a view.

to_world(cam, (x, y)) turns a pixel into a world point. A pixel fixes a ray, and the depth along it comes from one of three sources. The first is a horizontal plane at a height the model gives (a rim, a slot, the table). The second is the same point picked in a second picture: the two rays are intersected, and a gap of more than about 5 mm between them reveals a mismatch [34]. The third is the surface under the pixel. This is the table, a measured object, or a level patch that is matched between cameras by zero-mean normalized cross-correlation over candidate heights, a plane sweep [23]. Every result reports how far one pixel of picking error moves the point, and it warns when the pixel shows the robot’s own arm.

LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 render a depth picture with every camera. There the same calls back-project a mask’s pixels through the depth picture and merge the points of all cameras that see the object. An oriented box on the floor plan gives the centre, size and grasp yaw, and the lowest and highest points give the height. Only the visible surface is measured, so when the cameras see an object from one side only, its centre leans toward them by up to half its depth. For pinch grasps, a circle fitted to the depth points around a round dish gives the outer edge of its rim. RoboTwin 2.0 renders depth as well, but in all our RoboTwin runs perception used only the colour pictures and the camera models, as on RoboDojo. On these three benchmarks the robot’s own pixels come from the renderer’s segmentation of the robot’s parts, not from its meshes.

Measured objects keep their id for the whole episode. Measuring an object again looks for it where it was last seen, or where the gripper has taken it, and falls back on its earlier height when only one camera sees it now. The RoboDojo prompt gives the model the errors to expect. From the start pictures, low box-like objects (blocks, tiles, small flat things) usually come out within a few millimetres. Round, hollow or tall objects (balls, bowls, cups, bottles) are often 1–3 cm off, and too high or too large rather than too low. A wrist camera held about 25 cm above the object, together with the head camera, brings the error to 1–2 mm. Pixels read from an enlarged crop are about twice as precise as pixels read from the whole picture.

E.4 Motion

On RoboDojo, HexaShell runs as a policy inside the benchmark’s own evaluation client, which asks for one action at a time. While the model thinks, the policy answers “wait”, so the simulation stands still and no step is used. On the other three benchmarks the simulator runs in a server process with its own Python environment and talks to HexaShell over a socket.

On RoboDojo and RoboTwin 2.0 the arms are ARX X5 arms and take joint targets. HexaShell solves inverse kinematics itself, with Levenberg–Marquardt steps on the 6-D pose error of the grasp point from several starting configurations. Of the solutions that keep the arm out of the table, it takes the one with the least joint travel. A straight path is solved waypoint by waypoint, and a swing is checked for table clearance along the way. Motions follow a trapezoid-like speed profile, so long moves across the table take fewer steps while the last centimetres of a descent stay slow. A short description of the rig (where the arms stand, where the table is, how the gripper reading relates to the fingers) lets the same driver serve both benchmarks.

On LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 a Franka Panda runs under robosuite’s operational-space controller in delta mode. That controller lags a moving goal by about 0.16 s and does not compensate a held load. The adapter therefore plans a straight line on one speed profile and aims each step past the plan, by feeding forward the plan’s velocity and acceleration and slowly integrating what is left at rest. The same planner serves both benchmarks. On RoboCasa365 the arm also rides on a wheeled base.

E.5 Sandbox

The model’s cells run in a separate worker process with one persistent Python namespace, so variables and functions survive between cells. Every robot call is forwarded to the host process, which owns the arms, cameras and perception, and waits for the answer. After the worker has imported what it needs, it confines itself in three layers. Landlock limits file access to a few read-only trees (the Python installation, the HexaShell package and system libraries) and the worker’s own workspace, and it blocks every TCP connection. Seccomp forbids network sockets where Landlock cannot block them, new programs and processes, and signals to or tracing of other processes. At the Python level, imports are limited to a list of modules (numpy, math, cv2, json and similar) and open to the workspace. These last limits give clear error messages but are not the boundary. A cell may use a limited amount of CPU time; waiting for robot calls does not count. The simulator, the task code, the layouts, the skills’ sources and the network are therefore out of reach whatever a cell does.

E.6 Writing the skills

Skills are written from the records of earlier runs and, where HexaShell-TaskTools had tools for a task, from what those tools had shown. Each claim carries its evidence. On the three newer benchmarks this is the number of episodes it was seen in, such as “(7 eps)”, or a mark for a probe, a scripted test, a HexaShell-TaskTools tool, or “untested”. RoboDojo skills name the development round and layouts instead, such as “R0 8/8” or “(l0)”. A checking script enforces the rules of Section 2.4 together with the format. On the three newer benchmarks a skill has at most 45 lines of 100 characters. On RoboTwin 2.0 the skills use only the instruction wording of the learning runs, never the unseen wording of the test. The RoboDojo skills went through four versions during the development rounds on layouts 0–9 of seed 0. The skills cite only learning and validation episodes.

Table 15 gives the sizes of the skills, one per task; RoboDojo’s eight Open tasks and 85 of the LIBERO-PRO tasks have none. The median skill has 39 to 61 lines and 2.4 to 4.3 thousand characters, about one page. Only three of the 205 skills contain code: a five-line loop in RoboDojo’s press-by-number skill, and reference code in its insert-key and fill-egg-holder skills. The insert-key skill, with 689 lines, is the one long skill; the next longest has 138 lines.

Table 16 divides the characters of each benchmark’s skills among their sections and counts the evidence marks as they are written in the skills. The largest part of every benchmark’s skills is the flow, 31 to 56% of the characters. Common failures with their fixes come next (15–23%), then what counts as done (9–21%), verified numbers (10–15%) and step costs (5–9%). The skills of the three newer benchmarks cite their evidence: 932 to 1,136 episode counts per benchmark, such as “(7 eps)”, which name 5,928 to 7,776 episodes in all; the episodes are summed over all marks, so one episode can count several times. LIBERO-PRO’s skills also cite 513 probes, short tests run for a skill, and RoboCasa365’s 6 probes, 50 scripted tests and 140 results of HexaShell-TaskTools’s tools. The RoboDojo skills cite development rounds and layouts instead, such as “R0 8/8” or “(l0)”. Claims without evidence are marked as untested, 10 to 71 per benchmark. On RoboDojo 19% of the characters are code, nearly all of it the reference code of insert key and fill egg holder.

Appendix F Robot API reference

Tables 17 and 18 give the RoboDojo API as part 3 of its prompt describes it to the model. The other benchmarks share these calls and add those named in Section E.2. Cameras are head, left_wrist and right_wrist, and arms are left and right. Motion calls use steps and return when the motion is done; the other calls use none. A Thing is a measured object, a Mask an outline in one picture and a Spot a world point. Every result prints as one line or a few, with a warning first when there is one (Fig. 3), and its fields can be used in code. Errors are Python exceptions whose message says what to change.

The RoboDojo system prompt has six parts (Table 19), 35 thousand characters in all. A seventh part, which explains the remembered findings of Env_ICL, is left out in every run of this report. shows the task card of one episode of press by number, without its three start pictures. The task’s skill follows it in the prompt ().

, and  give three skills in full, as the model reads them: the two RoboDojo skills of Sections 3.4 and I.3 and one RoboTwin 2.0 skill in the shorter format of the three newer benchmarks. Appendix I Episode analysis

This section looks inside the RoboDojo runs, which have a run without skills and the most detailed records: the two runs of Table 3 and, in a few places, the runs at effort high of Table 14.

I.1 Picture code written by the agent

measure takes words or a pixel itself and asks SAM 3 for the outline, so the agent seldom needs find first. We count the episodes in which any cell reads a raw picture (robot.image) or calls OpenCV. Without skills these are 10.3% (105 of the 1,019 episodes with a record), and 60 of them belong to push T and swap T, the two tasks with T-shaped blocks. Deposit coin and insert tubes add 10 each. With skills the share is 9.8%. The insert-key skill contains picture code (30 episodes), push T’s skill suggests a colour mask for the target pad (22), and deposit coin adds 15. Without insert key the share with skills is 7.1%. In the runs at effort high the agent wrote such code less often, in about 4% of the episodes with or without skills.

I.2 Endings, slips and infrastructure

Table 20 sorts the episodes of each run by how they ended. Success is reported by the benchmark’s checker; the agent cannot declare it. A failed episode is ended by the benchmark (Env.), nearly always because the step budget was spent, by the limit on replies or time (Limit), or by the agent with finish, for one of three reasons: no_budget when the steps left cannot pay for another attempt (Budget), keep_partial when another attempt would put a partial result at risk (Partial), and stuck when it sees no way forward (Stuck). For RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0 our records give only the sum of the three. The RoboDojo rows are the two runs of Table 3 on the 34 tasks outside Open, and the RoboCasa365 rows the two runs of Table 4.

The agent ends most failed episodes itself, and seldom early. On RoboDojo with skills it ended 125 of the 156 failures with finish, 99 of them because the steps left could not pay for another attempt, with a median of 22 steps left. The benchmark ended 28, nearly all at the step budget, and 3 reached the limit on replies or time. Without skills the agent ended 248 of the 353 failures itself, 226 of them for lack of steps (a median of 14.5 left), and the benchmark ended 102. In both runs, failed episodes used a median of 97–99% of their step budget and successful ones about half. Most failures are partial: 239 of the 353 without skills and 124 of the 156 with them earned part of the task’s score. On RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0 the agent also ended most failures itself. On LIBERO-PRO, whose step limits are short, 38 of the 51 failures reached the limit.

We count the episodes in which a motion raised Dropped. Without skills, 289 of the 1,019 episodes with a record had a slip; 28% of them still succeeded, against 80% of the episodes without one. With skills, 153 of the 1,020 had a slip (46% against 91%). The skills thus make slips rarer, through grasp heights and openings that held in earlier runs, and they help the agent recover from one, but a slip still costs much of the chance of success. With skills, 82 of the 156 failures had a slip, and 68 of these come from six tasks, led by store laptop and headphones (22 of its 29 failures) and hang mugs (13 of 23). In 106 failures a motion stopped against something (Blocked), and 37 had neither a slip nor a block. Most of these 37 missed an exact final placement: deposit coin (10), where the coin did not go into the slot, insert key (9), and fold clothes (6), where the fold stayed uneven. Without skills, 208 of the 353 failures had a slip, 224 a block and 76 neither, and all 30 failures of store laptop and headphones had a slip.

In the run without skills, 58 episodes were started again: 49 because the simulator hung at its start (32 at an error dialog, 17 silent for 30 minutes), on GPUs shared with other users’ jobs, and 9 because no episode began. An episode is started again only when a run gave no verdict, and each episode counts once, with its last finished run. Two episodes that hung three times on one machine were finished on another, and no episode was given up. One success ended without a result file and is counted from the benchmark’s log. The first run with skills needed 17 restarts. In the two runs, 1.9% and 2.1% of the model requests failed at the gateway and were sent again, which costs time but no steps.

I.3 Press by number

Two number cards stand behind two red buttons. The agent must press the left red button as many times as the left card shows, then the blue button once, then the middle red button as many times as its card shows and the blue button once more, and bring both arms home. Without a skill, at effort high, it succeeded in 23 of 30 episodes. All seven failures ended suddenly while the agent was pressing, between steps 54 and 353 of the 700 allowed. A press too many ends the episode at once, and in several of these records the agent had made a test press to find the depth, or repeated presses it was unsure of. The skill has 42 lines. It says that every move down to a grasp height of 0.80 m counts as a full press, BLOCKED or not, and must never be repeated. It gives the depth, since 0.79 m sometimes pried the closed fingers open and flung the arm, and the loop below, which prints the count after every press:

⬇
for i in range(n):
d = robot.goto(arm, (x, y, 0.80), pitch=90, yaw=0, roll=0, path='line', contact=True)
print('presses done:', i + 1, d)
u = robot.goto(arm, (x, y, 0.85), pitch=90, yaw=0, roll=0, path='line')
if not u.ok: break # failed lift = arms touching or arm thrown off (6/6): look

With the skill the task passed all 30 episodes at both efforts. The failures without the skill came from counting, and the skill’s rule addresses them: count every press once, and never press again to be sure. At effort xhigh, however, the agent without a skill also passed 29 of 30, so there the higher effort did most of what the rule does. The skill still shortens the episodes: at xhigh a success took a median of 162 steps with it and 247 without (153 and 265 at high). Appendix J shows one episode with the skill at effort high, with five cells, 109 steps and 86 seconds. The skill’s only code is the loop above, which the agent would otherwise write itself.

I.4 Store tools in toolbox

This Open task has no skill. The agent must put a hammer, a wrench, a pair of pliers and a tape measure into a toolbox. It passed none of the 30 test episodes and none of the 10 development episodes of round R0. In R0, 66 of the 84 grasps that closed on a tool slipped: 46 of 48 on the hammer and the wrench, 19 of 24 on the pliers and 1 of 12 on the tape measure. The attempts that slipped took half of all steps (4,419 of 8,892). The pictures show how. The agent grips a long tool near its middle, as the prompt advises; as the arm lifts, the tool turns about the axis between the fingertips until it hangs, and then slides out between the pads. Most slips (48 of 66) came within the first six steps of a move. A general change to the prompt’s parts on acting and checking and to how results print did not help (0 of 30 again). In scripted tests outside the agent, with each tool’s place taken from the benchmark’s demonstration video, the tape measure, the wrench and the hammer could each be placed (4 of 4, 6 of 6 and 2 of 3), but the pliers never (0 of about 45), and no scripted run placed all four (0 of 12). What this task lacks is a grasp that holds the long tools with this gripper, more than knowledge that a skill could add.

I.5 Cost

Table 21 gives the mean cost of a RoboDojo episode over the 1,020 test episodes of the 34 tasks outside Open, in the two runs of Table 3; one episode without skills has no record and is left out. Prompt tokens are summed over all requests of an episode, most of them read from the gateway’s cache, and output tokens include the reasoning tokens. The skills cut the turns by 17% and the steps by 19%, and an episode needs fewer robot calls and pictures and 44% fewer reasoning tokens. The agent follows a flow that worked instead of searching for one. The wall times compare only roughly, since the gateway was slower during parts of the run without skills.

Per request, xhigh reasons longer. With skills, over 21,703 pairs of requests made at the same turn of the same episode at high and at xhigh, the reasoning tokens rise 2.4 times (59.5 to 143.8 on average) and all output tokens 1.6 times, while the time per request stays about the same (16.1 and 15.6 s). A request carries 22 to 25 thousand prompt tokens, 89–90% of them read from the gateway’s cache. Without skills (26,280 pairs) the reasoning tokens rise 3.3 times and a request takes twice as long, though the gateway was slower during parts of that run. On RoboCasa365 with skills, xhigh costs 3.7 times the reasoning tokens per episode (2,711 against 740) and 6% more time (543 against 510 s).

shows an episode of press by number from the RoboDojo run with skills at effort high, seed 0 and layout 14, the task card of . Each cell is followed by what it printed. Appendix K Real-robot details

The URAI adapter connects the API to two PiPER-X arms with a head camera and two wrist cameras, all RGB-D. URAI [32], a separate service, plans and executes every motion: inverse kinematics, collision checking, time scaling and execution. For each goto the adapter sends URAI the target, asks for a planning-only preview of the whole trajectory, and executes it if the plan is accepted. With path="auto" it tries a straight line first. Otherwise it accepts a joint-space path only if the path stays within 3 cm of the line and no more than 1 cm below its end points. A refused plan raises NotExecuted as in simulation, and a grasp that closes on nothing raises Dropped. Steps are counted as executed time in units of 0.04 s, so a step budget buys about as much robot time as on RoboDojo.

The adapter has no segmentation service at present, so find, measure and things are absent. The model reads pixels off the pictures, with a grid or an enlarged crop, and to_world turns each pixel into a point. It uses the measured depth first, then a plane at a height the model gives, then a second view. The model checks a point by projecting it back with to_pixel and marking it in a new picture. The robot’s own pixels come from URAI’s collision capsules, projected into each picture and compared with the measured depth.

The real-robot prompt keeps the six parts of Section 2.3 in 11,110 characters of English. A real robot has no checker, so finish has one more status, done. The model’s report is stored with the episode. The adapter has 907 lines. The loop, the sandbox and the geometry of to_world above it are the code that runs the simulated benchmarks. The adapter’s 29 end-to-end tests pass against URAI’s kinematic simulator.

The block tasks run as a loop in which each task leaves the scene for the next, and for the pens and plush toys a person resets the scene by hand before each episode. The block tasks also have more episodes on record than Table 6 shows. Over all finished episodes, shuffling reaches 10 of 11, language sorting 10 of 12, stacking 18 of 23 and unstacking 14 of 21. The one stacking failure in the table ended when the supervising model saw a person in a wrist camera and stopped the episode before the robot had moved, so it may be a false stop.

On all nine tasks, a second model supervises each episode and gives a verdict from fresh pictures and arm feedback.11 1 GPT-6.1-Terra writes the code, supervised by GPT-6-Astra. The counts come from these records; we did not review every episode by hand, and prompts and supervision rules changed between episodes. The papaya take-out count keeps two failures from a bug that gave the task to the wrong arm and one from a supervisor time-out, both since fixed.

Cover blocks runs on a third PiPER-X robot. All 53 finished episodes succeed; Table 6 counts the last ten.

Figure 15 shows the PiPER-X setup from above, in two episodes run earlier by HexaShell-TaskTools (Section 3.4), whose tools use only RGB pictures, the cameras’ calibration and the state of the arms. Figure 5 shows one episode of HexaShell for each task.
